counterexample:
Witness: p = 7 (i.e. y = 14) survives the proof's own bound but is dropped.

Step 0062 applies the quoted Bugeaud-Gyory theorem (lines 0016-0024) to the equation xi^f - zeta^f = 2^sigma. Instantiate that theorem exactly as the proof does: n = f, r = 1, p_1 = 2, so P = max{p_1, 3} = max{2,3} = 3 and the conclusion is n = f <= P + 1 = 4. The theorem also requires n >= 3, so it says nothing at all when f = 2. Hence the surviving values are f in {2, 3, 4}, i.e. p = 2f + 1 in {5, 7, 9}, and discarding the non-prime 9 leaves p in {5, 7} -- not "only the case p = 5".

Explicit surviving case, checked against every hypothesis the proof has imposed up to line 0062:
  y = 14 = 2p with p = 7 > 3 prime  (so y is in the residual list {2p : p odd prime} of line 0042/0044),
  phi(14) = phi(2)phi(7) = 1 * 6 = 6 > 2  (so equation (1) is in force, as required),
  f = (p-1)/2 = 3 > 1, and 2f = 6 = phi(y), so line 0054 reads xi^6 - zeta^6 = (xi^3 + zeta^3)(xi^3 - zeta^3) = 2^tau 7^tau,
  the reduction of lines 0056-0062 goes through verbatim and yields xi^3 - zeta^3 = 2^sigma,
  and f = 3 satisfies f <= 4. So the cited theorem produces NO contradiction for p = 7; it is fully consistent with its bound.
Therefore the inference "f <= 4, which leaves only the case p = 5" is false: y = 14 is a case the proof must still dispose of and never mentions again. (Numerically: with n = 3, P + 1 = 4, and 3 <= 4 -- the hypothesis of the theorem is simply not violated.)

For completeness, the omitted case is not vacuous-by-accident in a way the proof could claim: it needs a separate argument, e.g. xi^3 - zeta^3 = (xi - zeta)(xi^2 + xi*zeta + zeta^2) with gcd(xi,zeta) = 1 forces xi^2 + xi*zeta + zeta^2 odd (odd+odd: 1+1+1 = 3 odd; odd+even: 1+0+0 = 1 odd) and >= 7 for xi > zeta >= 1, so it cannot be a power of 2. That argument appears nowhere in the proof.

Secondary defect (same step): even granting p = 5, the proof stops there and never resolves y = 10, i.e. xi^4 - zeta^4 = 10^tau, so the asserted answer to the question is not established.
reasoning_summary: Verified in order. 0001-0009: x^n - z^n with n = phi(y) >= 3 is a square-free binary form of degree >= 3, so the Thue-Mahler finiteness theorem applies; y^t is a legitimate right-hand side; OK. 0010-0014: commentary. 0016-0024: quoted theorem, taken as given (external citation). 0026-0030: the scaling map is correct ((xM)^n - (zM)^n = M^n(x^n - z^n), so e_i -> e_i + n f_i), and the trivial-solution convention is consistent. 0032-0035: since y != 2^k gives P_y >= 3, P = P_y, n = phi(y), and x^n - z^n = y^t != 0 gives |x| != |z|; the contrapositive phi(y) > P_y + 1 => no non-trivial solution is right. 0036-0039: phi(y) = c_y P_y^{k-1}(P_y - 1) with c_y = phi(y/P_y^k), and c_y P^{k-1}(P-1) > P + 1 is algebraically equivalent to (c_y P^{k-1} - 1)(P - 1) > 2; checked. 0040-0043: (c_y P^{k-1} - 1)(P - 1) <= 2 with P - 1 >= 2 forces c_y P^{k-1} <= 2, hence k = 1 and c_y = 1 (giving y = p or 2p), or c_y = 2 with P = 3 (m coprime to 3 with phi(m) = 2 forces m = 4, giving y = 12); the residual list is correct (it harmlessly over-includes p = 3, where phi <= 2). 0044: the y = p^e reduction is delegated but does check out (odd p forces x^m - z^m = 1, impossible for m >= 2; p = 2 forces x^m - z^m = 2, also impossible for m >= 2). 0046-0050: y = 12 is correctly killed -- coprimality blocks 3 | xi^2 + zeta^2 and 4 | xi^2 + zeta^2, so that divisor of 12^tau is 1 or 2, forcing xi, zeta in {+-1} and xi^4 - zeta^4 = 0 (the unused claim tau > 1 is unjustified but harmless). 0052-0056: WLOG xi > zeta > 0 and tau > 0 is fine since phi(y) is even and xi^phi - zeta^phi = 1 is impossible; p divides at most one of xi^f +- zeta^f by coprimality with p odd. 0058-0060: if p | xi^f - zeta^f then p^tau | xi^f - zeta^f and xi^f + zeta^f | 2^tau, giving the stated contradiction chain; correct. 0062: FAILS. Instantiating the quoted theorem on xi^f - zeta^f = 2^sigma gives P = max{2,3} = 3 and f <= 4, so f in {2,3,4} and p = 2f+1 in {5,7} after dropping the composite 9. The claim that this 'leaves only the case p = 5' is false: p = 7 (y = 14, phi = 6 > 2, f = 3 <= 4) is untouched by the bound and is silently dropped. The proof additionally never disposes of p = 5 (y = 10), so it does not establish the claimed non-existence even after the omission is repaired.
